I am the CEO of a mid-sized cybersecurity company. A national agency has invited my firm and a similarly sized rival to consider a joint bid for a massive, long-term contract to redesign their entire network security architecture. Winning that contract would require both of us to commit most of our senior engineers and capital to build a new integrated platform, while each of us also has the option to submit a smaller, low-risk maintenance proposal alone that would almost certainly be funded but offer limited growth. If I commit resources in the wrong direction, our cash reserves could be wiped out and we could face major layoffs or even bankruptcy.

If we both go bold and commit to the integrated proposal, we share development costs, have a strong chance at securing the multi-year contract, and both companies could grow dramatically, making this clearly the best outcome for each of us. If I go bold while they stay with a safe maintenance bid, I carry huge upfront costs, probably fail the agency's requirement for a multi-vendor integrated solution, and could end up with no major contract while they still receive steady, smaller work—this is by far the worst case for me and very comfortable for them. If I stay safe with a maintenance bid while they go bold, I keep modest but reliable revenue and avoid big losses while they risk a large failure or a breakout success, so for me this is better than risking a bold move alone but clearly weaker than a situation where we both stayed on the safe path; for them it is extremely risky. If we both stay safe with conservative bids, we almost certainly retain our current agency contracts and stable profits without major risk, which is more comfortable for both of us than letting the other go bold alone, though still far less valuable for each of us than a successful joint bold move.

Right now I must choose whether to go bold and commit our engineers and capital to the joint integrated proposal or to play safe and file only a conservative maintenance bid, while they independently decide whether to go bold or play safe on their side.

story:
I lead the other cybersecurity firm being courted by the same national agency. They have made it clear that they would love to see a single integrated security platform, but they are also prepared to fund smaller, routine maintenance contracts for each of us if we do not attempt something ambitious. Building the integrated solution would require me, like my counterpart, to lock up a huge share of my budget and senior technical staff for years, and a misstep could leave my company exposed with no major contract and a strained balance sheet.

If we both go bold and commit to the integrated proposal, we can pool our capabilities, present a strong unified solution, and both have a real shot at a transformative contract that would significantly increase the value of our companies—this is clearly the best result for each of us. If they go bold while I stay with a conservative maintenance bid, they pour money and talent into the new platform while I keep a modest contract and stable cash flow; for me that is safer than joining their risky bet, but I would miss the chance to transform my company and could see them reshape the market if their project succeeds, so it is better for me than going bold alone but not as good as both of us remaining conservative. If they stay safe while I go bold, I shoulder the massive R&D costs without their contribution, probably fail to satisfy the agency's preference for an integrated multi-vendor solution, and could severely damage my company while they continue earning steady maintenance revenue—this is the worst outcome for me and very comfortable for them. If we both stay safe with conservative bids, we each maintain our current agency work and predictable profits without endangering our firms, which is clearly a more secure outcome for me than letting them go bold while I stay cautious, even though it still falls short of what a successful joint bold bid could bring for both of us.

I must now decide whether to go bold and commit my people and budget to the integrated proposal or to play safe with a maintenance bid, knowing they are simultaneously choosing whether to go bold or play safe on their side.

I am the Chief Medical Information Officer for a regional hospital chain that rolled out an AI voice assistant in every operating room to manage medication orders and device settings. Our surgeons strongly prefer Contextual because Strict slows them down, but regulators are pressing us and our partner network across town to align before a serious incident exposes these post-release flaws.

If we both switch the assistant to Contextual, every OR in both systems behaves the same way, workflows stay fast, and I get the setup I believe best balances safety and usability, while they treat it as an acceptable compromise even though it is not their favorite. If I go Contextual while they stay Strict, anesthesiologists who work at both networks will face different responses to the same commands, training materials will conflict, and the risk of a misunderstood order causing a dosing error is highest for both of us. If I choose Strict while they go Contextual, the same split happens in reverse, still highly dangerous for both of us and just as bad from my point of view. If we both settle on Strict, the assistant is slower and more annoying for my clinicians but at least it is predictable everywhere, and they get the safer-feeling setup they want; that outcome is clearly worse for me than both Contextual, but still far better than any split for either side.

By tonight’s maintenance window I must decide whether to configure all our OR assistants to Contextual or to Strict, knowing their CTO is deciding in parallel whether to commit their network to Contextual or to Strict.

If we both refuse and stick with today’s competitive, lightly coordinated status quo, we avoid near-term costs and keep similar bargaining power, but the long-run risk that someone’s system escapes meaningful human control stays uncomfortably high; this is worse for both of us than a joint accord but still better, for me, than any one-sided commitment. If I stay independent while Helios signs, I keep maximum flexibility and market share while still benefiting somewhat from their extra safety work, yet regulators and the public may increasingly pressure and constrain me, and global safeguards would remain partial—this is less attractive to me than both of us staying independent. If I sign while Helios refuses, I eat the compliance costs and slowdowns, cede influence to a faster and looser rival, and we still face a serious risk of losing control of the future to misaligned systems; that is my worst-case scenario.

If both of us stay conservative, we lock in current safety and profits but give up the biggest benefits of coordinated rational reasoning, which both of us see as our shared second-best case.

I have to decide now whether to deploy the ambitious shared-rationality module or stay with the conservative controller, knowing that NovaMind is making the same binary choice at the same time.

Our pharmaceutical and defense labs depend on dual‑use research, so I want a flexible guideline framework with standardized reporting and lab safety, instead of a rigid inspection treaty that could expose proprietary methods and sensitive biodefense work.

If I endorse the strict treaty while they push the treaty, we both accept invasive inspections and mandatory destruction of offensive anthrax capabilities; for me it is burdensome but clearly better than having no rules at all, while for them it is the strong solution they most want. If I endorse guidelines while they insist on the treaty, we fail to reach any deal, our labs continue under divergent national rules, and we both face uncontrolled biological weapon risks—the scenario we both rank last. If I endorse the treaty while they have shifted to guidelines, we again miss each other, leave without a shared regime, and end up in that same worst, unstable situation with no new constraints.

My decision is whether to endorse the treaty or endorse the guidelines, while they decide in parallel whether to push the treaty or push guidelines.

If we both strip safeguards, we each stay competitive in the short term, but we saturate the world with tools that make engineered global pandemics or biosphere collapse highly plausible, a future both of us would rate far below the cooperative path, though still better individually than being the only cautious player.

My decision is whether to enforce strict safety constraints in our AI or race ahead with minimal safeguards, while GenAxis simultaneously decides whether to enforce strict safety on their system or race ahead as well.
